overall_summary: Space-themed content, specifically focusing on extreme planetary anomalies, bizarre cosmic chemistry, and sensory space facts, significantly outperforms cognitive psychology and brain-related trivia. Short, punchy videos around 15-16 seconds with high-arousal curiosity hooks are driving the most engagement.

winning_patterns.pattern: Extreme Exoplanet Weather & Sensory Space Facts
winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet of Burning Ice Will Break Your Brain!' achieved 1,053 views, while 'What Does Outer Space Actually Smell Like?' reached 368 views, and 'The Planet Where It Rains Molten Iron!' secured 328 views with high relative like counts.
winning_patterns.action: Produce a series focusing on extreme exoplanet environments, cosmic anomalies, and sensory descriptions of space (smell, taste, touch) using vivid, high-contrast visual hooks.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'Sharks Are Older Than Trees?' (302 views) and 'This Animal Literally Dies Every Winter!' (179 views) show solid baseline performance compared to standard trivia.
winning_patterns.action: Incorporate mind-bending evolutionary paradoxes and extreme survival stories in the animal kingdom, emphasizing life-or-death stakes.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Is Hiding This From You' (38 views), 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' (17 views), and 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' (max 52 views) consistently struggle to gain traction.
weak_patterns.action: De-prioritize standard psychological facts and brain hacks. If covering brain science, pivot to extreme anomalies or sci-fi adjacent topics like AI brain-wave reconstruction.

next_video.concept: The Planet Where It Rains Liquid Sapphires and Rubies
next_video.opening_direction: Show a stunning visual of sparkling red and blue gems falling from a dark sky with the voiceover: 'There is a giant planet in our galaxy where it literally rains precious gems...'
next_video.twist_direction: '...but you would never survive to collect them, because the winds blow these liquid jewels at 5,000 miles per hour, shredding anything in their path.'
next_video.reason: Leverages the highly successful exoplanet weather pattern ('rains molten iron', 'rains glass sideways') by using high-value assets (rubies/sapphires) as a visual and psychological hook.

experiment: Test a 'What-If' space survival micro-narrative: 'What would happen to your body if you stepped onto the Planet of Burning Ice without a spacesuit?' to bridge the gap between space facts and cinematic survival storytelling.
